input.headline: The flicker of the mains-powered lights in this video matches the national grid on Sunday 8 November 2026 at about 11:49:38 UTC, not on Thursday 5 November at 13:19:37 as stated.
input.difference: About 2 days 22.5 hours later than stated (three days later, about 1 h 30 min earlier in the day)
input.what_it_means: The timing evidence does not support the stated recording time. The video fits the grid record on 8 November and fits nowhere special on 5 November. This tells you when the video was recorded. It does not explain why the stated time is different: it could be a wrong device clock, a mislabelled file, or something else. Find out how the stated time was produced before drawing any conclusions about anyone.
findings: Scene: a dim indoor room lit only by ceiling strip lights. There is no window and no on-screen clock, so the lights are the only timing source.
The light flicker carried a strong signal that behaves like the grid, usable for 65% of the clip. The audio hum was weak (24% usable), so I used the flicker.

On the stated day (5 Nov), the best match was 10:03:40 with a score of 0.915. That is ordinary background level, matched by chance fits on every day from 29 Oct to 11 Nov (0.89–0.925). Nothing matched near 13:19.
Searching a week either side, one match stood well above the rest: 8 Nov 2026 at 11:49:38 UTC, score 0.987. The next-best rival scored 0.925.

It passed all three checks. Score sharpness: the score falls away within seconds and drops to about 0.6–0.7 at ±60 s. Split halves: the two halves of the clip each point to the same start, 11:49:36 and 11:49:39. Rival days: the margin over the best other day is 0.062.
Both halves agree to within 3 seconds, so there is no sign of splicing within the excerpt.
The reference was Elexon's 15-second grid data, which is coarser than the 1-second archive (not available for November 2026). The match is still clear-cut.
